10.1002_adfm.77378: Ionic liquids (ILs) have emerged as attractive bulk modifiers for perovskite absorbers in realizing long‐term operational stability; however, most IL anions are chemically “one‐sided”, typically neutralizing only cationic or anionic vacancies. Our study introduces a novel strategy using ILs with amphoteric anions—specifically tetramethylguanidine hydrogen sulfate (GUHS) and tetramethylguanidine dihydrogen phosphate (GUDHP)—to act as “universal passivators”. The amphoteric nature of HSO 4 − and H 2 PO 4 − anions passivate both Lewis acidic and Lewis basic defects via localized electron‐rich oxygen sites and electron‐deficient regions, while the guanidine cation anchor FA + /MA + cations through multiple N─H⋯N bonds, resulting in a high‐quality perovskite film with suppressed defect densities, enhanced crystallization, and relieved residual strain. The passivation effect is more pronounced in GUDHP than in GUHS due to the higher basicity of H 2 PO 4 − ‐derived PO 4 framework and presence of multiple P─OH functionalities. Consequently, the GUDHP‐modified PSCs achieve a PCE of 26.13% with an FF exceeding 85% for normal bandgap (1.56 eV) cells, and a remarkable 20.06% PCE with an impressive 85.74% FF for wide bandgap (1.84 eV) devices. In addition, the GUDHP‐modified devices maintained 93.6% of their initial PCE after 1000 h of continuous operation under the ISOS‐L‐1 protocol.
10.1002_adma.202518490: The advancement of high-energy-density lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) is hindered by the chemical instability of both lithium-metal anode and high-nickel layered oxide cathodes. While cathode-to-anode crossover is well-documented, the reverse process of anode-to-cathode crossover remains underexplored. Here, we systematically investigate such crossovers and the degradation pathway in pouch cells with a localized high-concentration electrolyte, comparing NMC622, NMC811, and NMC90 cathodes paired with lithium-metal and graphite anodes. Despite delivering higher initial capacities, LMBs exhibit faster capacity fade under long-term cycling at 45 °C. To isolate cathode-side degradation, galvanostatic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (GEIS) measurements of cycled cathodes paired with delithiated lithium iron phosphate (LFP) counter electrodes reveal significantly higher charge-transfer resistance in cathodes cycled with lithium-metal. Surface characterization via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) reveals greater electrolyte decomposition on cathodes cycled with lithium metal, leading to thicker, more organic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphases (CEIs), consistent with the elevated charge-transfer resistance observed in GEIS measurements. Notably, NMC90 shows the most pronounced CEI thickening, linking higher cathode surface reactivity to greater susceptibility to anode-to-cathode crossover. This work presents compelling evidence of crosstalk degradation originating from lithium-metal anodes and underscores the importance of cross-interface stability for the design of durable LMBs.
10.1016_j.est.2026.124011: Additive manufacturing offers unprecedented opportunities to tailor alloy microstructures; however, the long-term corrosion behaviour of additively manufactured Ni-based superalloys in molten salt environments remains insufficiently understood. In this study, the hot corrosion behaviour of PBF-LB-produced Inconel 718 was investigated in molten Solar Salt with emphasis on the role of post-processing heat treatments and prolonged exposure. Specimens in the as-built, solution-annealed, and double-aged conditions were exposed for up to 900 h and characterized using mass loss measurements, X-ray diffraction, electron backscatter diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and cross-sectional SEM–EDS analysis. The as-built condition exhibited predominantly surface-limited oxidation with extremely thin oxide layers and negligible inward corrosion penetration, which is attributed to the retained cellular substructure and associated microsegregation that disrupt continuous diffusion pathways for aggressive species. In contrast, solution annealing activated grain-boundary-assisted degradation, resulting in thick but chemically unstable oxide scales and significant inward corrosion propagation with increasing exposure time. Localized Cr-depleted, Ti/Al–O-enriched reaction zones and near-surface void formation further indicate the breakdown of protective oxide behaviour in the solution-annealed state. Double aging moderated the corrosion response through γ' and γ″ precipitation, as confirmed by TEM analysis, which stabilizes the microstructure and limits the development of continuous grain-boundary corrosion pathways. Quantitative analysis shows that oxide thickness alone is not a reliable indicator of corrosion resistance. Although the phase assemblage of corrosion products becomes increasingly similar with prolonged exposure, post-processing treatments strongly influence time-dependent corrosion response, morphology, and spatial distribution of degradation.
